newsitem.title: USA: US House panel debates transportation fund renewal.
newsitem.headline: US House panel debates transportation fund renewal.

text.p: The U.S. Congress launched debate on Wednesday on rewriting its five-year-old federal transportation spending law, with lawmakers offering a number of different solutions.

Rep. John Kasich and Sen. Connie Mack urged the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee's subcommittee on surface transportation to repeal the law's controversial highway funding formula, which hinges on a 14 cent per gallon federal gasoline tax.

Instead, Congress should make road construction and tax collection for road repairs a job for states, said Kasich, a Republican from Ohio, and Mack, a Florida Republican, who originally offered the bill last year.

Wednesday's hearing was the first in the 105th Congress by a House or Senate Committee on reauthorization of the Intermodal Surface Transportation Efficiency Act of 1991, known as ISTEA. The law expires on September 30.
U.S. Reps. Tom DeLay, a Republican from Texas, and Gary Condit, a California Democrat, called for an overhaul of the current law's complex formula for distributing highway trust funds to the states.
States use the funds to back municipal bond offerings for roads, bridges and other infastructure projects.
The Delay-Condit bill, called STEP 21, would give back to states at least 95 percent of funds they kick in to the trust fund. Currently, many states receive considerably less.
The bill also would consolidate the many existing highway programs into two, and give states more spending flexibility, Delay and Conduit said.
They originally introduced the plan in the 104th Congress and reintroduced the measure earlier this week.
But New Jersey Governor Christine Todd Whitman warned that STEP 21 would shift over $1 billion of transportation funds annually out of New Jersey and 14 other states.

She opposed major changes in the current funding formula. "I urge you to build on the accomplishments of ISTEA, not abandon them," said Whitman, whose state is part of a coalition called ISTEA WORKS seeking fewer changes in the law.
Republican Rep. Bud Shuster, of Pennsylvania, who chairs the House Transportation Committee, said his panel faces a "daunting" task in reauthorizing ISTEA.
"We have a transportation crisis in America," Shuster said. Highways and bridges are crumbling, yet more people are traveling, he said, warning that Congress has a major job ahead.
At the same time, however, Congress has a "golden opportunity" with ISTEA's reauthoriztion to provide Americans a better transportation system as the next century approaches, Shuster said.
He said it is a good idea to give states more flexibility in transportation spending, but "this is a national system" that requires cooperation.
But Kasich said if Congress trusts states enough to hand over control of welfare spending, there is no reason why Washington cannot entrust them with transportation spending.
"If we felt we could send welfare programs that affect children home (to states), we certainly can send programs that affect concrete," he said.

The Senate Environment and Public Works Committee's transportation and infrastructure subcommittee has scheduled its first hearing of the 105th Congress on ISTEA reauthoriation for 1400 EST/1900 GMT on February 13.

"With the October 1, 1997 deadline rapidly approaching, the sooner we get down to business and begin hearings on the issue the better," said subcommittee chairman Sen. John Chafee, a Rhode Island Republican.
